title: Rational coordinates do not select an ambient dimension
status: Classical mathematics with newly authored derivation or finite example and explicit scope
summary: The user asked whether different kinds of numbers could exist on two- or three-dimensional sheets. A coordinate embedding can place the same numbers in many ambient spaces without changing their algebra. Rational points on a circle give a stronger example: exact rational coordinates can lie densely on a curved geometric object.
definitions: Q² is the set of ordered pairs of rationals; Q⊂R can also be placed in R³ by q↦(q,0,0). These are different choices of ambient coordinates.

result.name: Rational coordinates do not select an ambient dimension
result.statement: P(t) is a rational point on x²+y²=1. Every rational point except (−1,0) arises this way. Q² is countable and dense in R², while R is uncountable; none of these facts makes rationals inherently two-dimensional or reals inherently three-dimensional.
result.proof: Squaring and adding the coordinates of P(t) gives [(1−t²)²+4t²]/(1+t²)²=1. Conversely a rational point with x≠−1 has t=y/(1+x), and substitution using x²+y²=1 recovers the two coordinates. Rational t values are dense in R, and continuity of P makes these rational points dense in the circle except for the limiting missing point, which is approached as |t| grows. Countability of Q² follows by enumerating pairs of a countable set, while density follows by choosing a rational number in each coordinate interval. A set injection into an ambient space makes no claim about linear or topological equivalence.

example.calculation: The circle point is (7/25,24/25), with squared coordinates summing to one. The same pair can be displayed as (7/25,24/25,0) in R³, and the rational number 7/25 can be displayed on a line in either R² or R³. Its rationality has not changed. As Q-vector spaces, however, Q and Q² have dimensions one and two, so a mere enumeration is not a Q-linear isomorphism. The rational subspace topology also matters: no nonempty interval of R is countable, whereas every subset of Q is countable. Dense placement consequently does not make Q an open one-dimensional real manifold or turn a rational sheet into a continuous plane.

title: The circle is irreducible and its radius scaling has a contravariant map
status: Classical mathematics with newly authored derivation or finite example and explicit scope
summary: The historical answer invoked circle coordinate rings, prime ideals and scaling. A point prime is not the same thing as an irreducible component, and a map of spaces acts in the opposite direction on coordinate functions. Both distinctions can be checked in this small example.
definitions: Let A=R[x,y]/(x²+y²−1) and B=R[u,v]/(u²+v²−4).

result.statement: The defining polynomial is irreducible over R and generates a prime ideal, so A is a domain. The scaling φ is an algebraic isomorphism with inverse division by two, and its pullback is well defined. The point ideal (x−1,y) in A is maximal but does not define an extra irreducible component.
result.proof: If x²+y²−1 factored nontrivially over R, its degree two would force two affine-linear factors. Their highest homogeneous parts would multiply to x²+y², which has no real linear factor: a nonzero real direction cannot make a sum of two squares vanish identically along a line. Substituting into B’s relation gives 4x²+4y²−4=0 in A; substituting x↦u/2,y↦v/2 gives the inverse homomorphism. The quotient of A by (x−1,y) is R, proving maximality.

Meanwhile the zero ideal of the domain A describes its single generic irreducible component; individual point ideals provide locations within that component. Evaluation at a real circle point is a surjective algebra map to R whose kernel is the ideal of coordinate functions vanishing there. The quotient is R, hence that ideal is maximal. This is why a point ideal and the zero ideal describing the irreducible component carry different information.

title: An additive correction ansatz does not identify a new mechanism
status: Classical mathematics with newly authored derivation or finite example and explicit scope
summary: The historical gyre fragment adds undefined corrections to beta functions, vacuum energy, a magnetic moment and a holographic entropy. The mathematically defensible development is an identifiability test: an additive symbol is a parametrization until a model defines it and independent information separates it from its baseline.
definitions: For one scalar observable let F(θ,g)=θ+g, with both θ and g unknown real parameters. Identifiability means different admissible parameters produce different observable predictions.

result.name: An additive correction ansatz does not identify a new mechanism
result.statement: With no further constraints, the scalar sum has a one-dimensional unidentifiable direction, and the four-observable sum has a four-dimensional one. Knowing the baseline independently can identify a residual, but does not by itself explain or predict that residual.
result.proof: For every real t, F(θ+t,g−t)=θ+g=F(θ,g). Thus each observed sum has an entire affine line of compatible parameter pairs. The Jacobian is[1,1], whose null space is span{(1,−1)} and whose rank is1. In four dimensions the derivative is[I₄ I₄], of rank4, with kernel{(v,−v):v∈R⁴}. This exactly matches the four-parameter family of indistinguishable decompositions. If θ is fixed by an independent calibrated model, then g=F−θ is algebraically determined by the observation. But this is a fitted residual: obtaining future values of g still requires a separately defined predictive rule, and uncertainty in θ propagates directly to uncertainty in the inferred g.
